x13: Chronic low back pain: which treatment should you start with?
x14: In the US OPTIMIZE study of 749 people with chronic low back pain, participants first received 8 weeks of physiotherapy or cognitive behavioural therapy; those who did not benefit enough switched treatments or moved to a mindfulness programme. At week 10, those who started with physiotherapy had slightly better day-to-day function, while pain levels were similar between the groups.
x15: Although the gains were modest, physiotherapy emerged as a reasonable first step. After one year there was no meaningful difference between the second-stage options; switching or adding treatments later made little difference to the long-term outcome.
x16: Source: Annals of Internal Medicine, 20 April 2026
x18: Electrical stimulation after spinal cord injury: hope and reality
x19: In a small US study, 3 people with complete spinal cord injury had electrodes placed below and above the injury. Stimulation below the injury activated the leg muscles, while stimulation above it gave feedback on knee angle and stepping through signals felt in the chest, arm or back; the participants walked on a treadmill with a harness and a therapist’s support. In the international eWALK study of 48 people, however, stimulation delivered through the skin gave no extra benefit on top of 12 weeks of walking training.
x20: The main message of eWALK: walking training on its own clearly improved walking, even in people who had lived with a spinal cord injury for a long time. Stimulation technologies are promising, but they do not yet replace rehabilitation.
x21: Sources: Nature Biomedical Engineering, March 2026 · eClinicalMedicine, 2026
x23: Changing the way you walk in knee osteoarthritis
x24: In a study of 68 people with osteoarthritis on the inner side of the knee, motion analysis was used to decide for each participant whether turning the toes 5 or 10 degrees inwards or outwards would help more, followed by 6 sessions of gait training. Over one year, pain fell by an average of 2.5 points out of 10 (1.3 in the sham training group). MRI findings suggested that cartilage breakdown progressed more slowly.
x25: This is not a one-size-fits-all tip like “turn your toes in”; it needs individual measurement and expert guidance. The measurement will need to be simplified before the method can be widely used.

x50: A pig kidney became a bridge to a human kidney
x51: In the US, Tim Andrews, 66, who had end-stage kidney failure, received a kidney from a gene-edited pig. The kidney kept him off dialysis for 271 days, the longest period documented in a living recipient. When his immunosuppressive drugs were reduced because of an infection, the pig kidney was damaged and stopped working; in January 2026 Andrews received a human kidney from a donor, which started working straight away.
x52: Given how long organ waiting lists are, this is a hopeful step. For now, though, experience comes from only a small number of patients; the safety and durability of gene-edited pig kidneys are being studied in clinical trials.
x53: Sources: The Lancet, 9 September 2026 · Mass General Brigham
x56: CAR-T cell therapy for severe lupus
x57: CAR-T, a method used to treat cancer, is also being tried in diseases where the immune system attacks the body’s own tissues. In the CARLYSLE study run by University College London (UCL), immune cells from people with severe lupus were reprogrammed to target the B cells that drive the disease. In the lower-dose group, 5 of 6 patients went into remission by standard criteria, and those with kidney involvement lost less protein in their urine.
x58: There was no severe cytokine release syndrome and no nervous system side effects; liver injury in one patient resolved completely. These results come from an early study of 9 patients; a larger phase II study has started recruiting in the UK.
x62: AI support in mammography: results of the first randomised trial
x63: In the MASAI study of more than 105,000 women in Sweden, mammograms were read either with AI support or in the standard way by two radiologists. In the AI-supported group, 81% of cancers were caught at screening (74% in the standard group); there were 12% fewer cancers found between screening rounds and 27% fewer cancers of aggressive subtypes. False alarm rates were similar in both groups.
x64: AI is not replacing the radiologist but supporting them; interim results had shown a 44% reduction in radiologists’ reading workload. The study was done in a single country, with one device and one software system, and with experienced radiologists.
x65: Sources: The Lancet, 29 January 2026 · EurekAlert!
x66: Gene therapy for inherited deafness appears to last
x67: 42 people aged 9 months to 32 years with hearing loss caused by a fault in the OTOF gene had a harmless, modified virus carrying a healthy copy of the gene placed in the inner ear. In the study, run at eight centres in China, 90% of participants had better hearing at 2.5 years of follow-up, and more than half reached normal hearing levels. Children progressed from responding to sounds to speaking in short sentences and even singing.
x68: There were no serious side effects. The effect was strongest in people aged 18 and under; 10% of participants did not respond. The treatment is only for OTOF-related hearing loss, and the approval process is just beginning.
x69: Source: Nature, 22 April 2026 · Harvard Gazette
x70: Blocking small arteries for knee osteoarthritis pain (GAE)
x71: At Charité University Hospital in Berlin, 194 patients whose osteoarthritis pain had not improved with other treatments for at least 3 months had genicular artery embolisation: a thin catheter was used to deliver microspheres, which dissolve within a few hours, into small arteries around the knee. Median pain fell from 7 out of 10 to 3 at 12 months, and 80% of patients improved meaningfully.
x72: There were no moderate or severe side effects. However, this was a single-centre study without a control group, and only 79% of patients could be reached at 12 months. Exercise remains the cornerstone of treatment for knee osteoarthritis.
x74: Will AI read mammograms from now on?
x75: No. In the MASAI study in Sweden, AI was used to support radiologists, not replace them. With this approach, more cancers were caught at screening, cancers found between screening rounds fell by 12%, and the false alarm rate did not rise.
x76: Can pig organs be transplanted into people?
x77: It is still experimental. A gene-edited pig kidney transplanted into a patient in the US kept him off dialysis for 271 days and then became a bridge to a human kidney transplant. The safety and durability of this approach are being studied in clinical trials.

x98: Fast typing at home with a brain–computer interface
x99: In the US BrainGate study, small electrodes were placed in the movement area of the brain of two participants, one with advanced ALS and one with a spinal cord injury at neck level. The system turned attempted finger movements into letters on a keyboard. One participant typed 22 words a minute in their own home with a word error rate of just 1.6%, and about 30 sentences were enough to set the system up.
x100: A big step in communication for people who cannot speak or use their hands. The device is still for research use only and requires brain surgery.

x103: Exercise after colon cancer saves lives
x104: In the CHALLENGE study of 889 people with colon cancer in 6 countries who had finished chemotherapy, one group joined a 3-year, coach-supported, personalised exercise programme (from brisk walking to group classes); the other group received health education only. At 5 years, 80% of the exercise group and 74% of the other group were cancer-free; at 8 years, survival was 90% versus 83%.
x105: In the exercise group, the risk of cancer returning, a new cancer or death was 28% lower, and the risk of death 37% lower. It is the first large randomised trial to show that exercise can be part of cancer treatment.
x106: Sources: New England Journal of Medicine, June 2025 · Oncology Central
x109: Insulin-producing cells made from stem cells for type 1 diabetes

x111: Immunosuppressive drugs are needed so that the cells are not rejected. Two patients in the study died, one from an infection linked to these drugs. Phase III studies are under way.
